medical.title: Wearable monitor improves diagnosis of heart rhythm disorders after fainting
medical.summary: Early ECG monitoring initiated in the emergency department (ED) has the potential to transform the care of thousands of patients who visit the ED with unexplained fainting.

medical.title: No significant evidence for protection against cardiovascular outcomes with metformin in heart failure
medical.summary: Metformin did not significantly affect the risk of cardiovascular outcomes in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and diabetes or at risk of diabetes. These were the main findings of the Met-HeFT trial and a meta-analysis presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026.

medical.title: An RNA molecule contributes to therapy resistance of triple negative breast cancer
medical.summary: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive type of breast cancer. Chemotherapy before or after surgery remains the standard treatment regimen for stage I–III TNBC. Only a small portion of patients can benefit from targeted therapy with PARP inhibitors because of BRCA mutations. However, resistance to chemotherapy or targeted therapy remains a major hurdle.

medical.title: Popular sweeteners may leave effects that last for generations
medical.summary: Two widely used zero-calorie sweeteners, sucralose and stevia, may have effects that linger far longer than the sweet taste itself. In mice, researchers found that both sweeteners altered the gut microbiome, reduced beneficial compounds produced by gut bacteria, and changed the activity of genes involved in metabolism and inflammation. Some of those changes were also detected in later generations that had never consumed the sweeteners themselves.

medical.title: Trial results favor prasugrel over ticagrelor after coronary stenting
medical.summary: Prasugrel reduced major cardiovascular events to the same extent as ticagrelor but with lower major bleeding after coronary stenting in patients with acute coronary syndromes, according to results from the SWITCH SWEDEHEART trial presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026 and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.

medical.title: T cell therapy shows promise in treating aggressive brain cancer
medical.summary: A new phase 1 clinical trial has found that an emerging immunotherapy is promising for treating recurrent glioblastoma, a highly aggressive and fatal brain cancer. Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy is a form of immunotherapy that modifies an individual's own T cells (a type of immune cell) so they are better able to recognize and destroy cancer cells. The new clinical trial, the results of which were published Aug. 6 in Nature Medicine, focuses on a form of CAR-T therapy that trains these immune cells to target a protein known as B7-H3, which is highly prevalent in most glioblastomas.

medical.title: Virtual monitoring matches clinic care for heart-device patients
medical.summary: A virtual e-health system (VIRTUES) was as safe and effective as standard care for monitoring the function of cardiac implantable electronic devices, with the benefits of cost savings and patient satisfaction. These were the main findings of the VIRTUES trials presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026.

medical.title: Targeting protein synthesis control regions may reduce seizures in genetic epilepsy
medical.summary: Targeting the control of protein synthesis in the KCNQ2 gene may serve as a potential disease-modifying strategy for patients with a genetic form of neonatal-onset epilepsy and impaired brain development, according to a Northwestern Medicine study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

medical.title: Scientists in France pinpoint why STING pathway hasn't been harnessed for cancer therapy yet
medical.summary: Deep within the cellular landscape, a quiet failure was taking place, impeding a potentially successful form of cancer treatment. For years, scientists hoped an essential part of the innate immune system that detects foreign DNA in cellular cytoplasm—the STING pathway—could be harnessed for use in cancer immunotherapy.

medical.title: Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth
medical.summary: A long-standing picture of brain evolution as newer, rational layers stacked on top of an ancient “lizard brain” may be deeply misleading. Researchers found that evolution instead appears to balance two competing styles of brain wiring, expanding one while shrinking the other depending on what an animal needs to survive.

medical.title: Professional gaming is brutal on the body—inside the growing field of treating esports injuries
medical.summary: Chinese esports player Jian "Uzi" Zi-hao was more than a star "League of Legends" player: He was so talented that his team structured its entire strategy around his abilities, funneling resources to him and another teammate, Shi "Ming" Sen-Ming, so the duo could lead the team to victory. Over the course of his career, he earned more than $500,000 in tournament prize money.

medical.title: Most women wear shoes that don't match their feet, study finds
medical.summary: Most women in a new RMIT University study wore shoe sizes that differed from the size indicated by their foot length, highlighting the limitations of conventional sizing systems in accounting for differences in foot width and shape. The study of 107 women found 72% wore a different size under U.S. sizing and 65% under EU sizing.

medical.title: New prediction tool could help increase uptake of heart failure medicines
medical.summary: A new heart failure (HF) treatment effect calculator could help overcome one of the largest barriers to effective heart failure care by predicting the expected effects of treatment on blood pressure, kidney function and potassium levels. The research, presented today at the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Congress and simultaneously published today in Nature Medicine, uses individual patient data from 38,753 participants across nine major heart failure trials.

medical.title: New guidelines aim to bring precision medicine to stroke rehabilitation
medical.summary: A University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM) stroke rehabilitation specialist helped develop new recommendations for studying molecular biomarkers associated with recovery from stroke. The new guidelines could help pave the way for precision rehabilitation approaches tailored to individual patients.

medical.title: Scientists find why the liver may not heal even after you stop drinking
medical.summary: Alcohol-related liver disease may trap damaged liver cells in a regenerative limbo, preventing the organ from rebuilding itself even after drinking stops. Researchers linked the problem to inflammation-driven RNA errors and identified a pathway that could potentially be targeted to restore liver repair.

medical.title: The unlikely rise of the sea shanty band
medical.summary: Sea shanties became an online craze, but these old working songs are doing more than filling dancefloors: they're connecting communities too The post The unlikely rise of the sea shanty band appeared first on Positive News .

medical.title: Scientists may have found a shortcut to calorie restriction’s anti-aging benefits
medical.summary: Moderate calorie restriction lowered an immune protein called C3 that appears to help drive chronic inflammation as the body ages. Blocking the same protein reduced age related inflammation in mice, raising the possibility that future treatments could mimic some benefits of calorie restriction without severe dieting.

medical.title: Turmeric compound may protect blood vessels from diabetes damage
medical.summary: A compound found in turmeric may help protect blood vessels from some of the damage caused by Type 1 diabetes. In rats, curcumin reduced inflammation, improved cellular signaling, and restored vascular health to levels resembling those of nondiabetic animals. The results hint at a possible new way to reduce the long-term cardiovascular risks of diabetes, but human trials are still needed.

medical.title: A missing color in indoor light may help prevent myopia
medical.summary: A wavelength of light largely missing from indoor LEDs may play an important role in protecting developing eyes from nearsightedness. Researchers found that indigo light completely prevented myopia in tree shrews, whose eyes share important similarities with human eyes. The discovery raises the possibility that future indoor lighting could be redesigned to more closely mimic sunlight and potentially reduce childhood myopia.

medical.title: Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells
medical.summary: Early-life stress may physically alter how DNA is packaged in the brain, leaving stress-related genes primed to activate more easily years later. In mice, researchers were able to block this effect, preventing the heightened anxiety and stress sensitivity that otherwise appeared in adulthood.

medical.title: This weight-loss hormone may protect the liver even without weight loss
medical.summary: A hormone already known for curbing appetite and supporting weight loss may have a surprising second job: protecting the liver from inflammation and scarring. Researchers at McMaster University found that GDF15 activates a previously unknown brain-to-liver pathway that triggers the release of glucocorticoids, helping calm immune activity in the liver.

medical.title: AI may know how you’ll respond to a vaccine before you get it
medical.summary: AI may be able to predict how strongly someone will respond to a vaccine before they receive it. By analyzing antibody patterns in more than 4,000 people, researchers found signs of “immune readiness” that helped distinguish strong responders from weak ones. Surprisingly, even some healthy people responded poorly, while some immunosuppressed people mounted strong responses.

medical.title: Scientists discover how gut bacteria “train” the intestine to fight inflammation
medical.summary: A compound made when gut bacteria break down dietary fiber may do more than briefly calm inflammation—it could leave a lasting protective “memory” in the gut. Northwestern Medicine researchers found that butyrate can reprogram intestinal lining cells so they continue encouraging anti-inflammatory immune responses even after the compound is gone. In mice, this effect boosted production of the immune-calming molecule IL-10 and reduced the severity of colitis-like disease.

medical.title: Ozempic does something unexpected to the brain’s hunger neurons
medical.summary: Ozempic may work in the brain in almost the opposite way scientists expected, activating hunger-linked neurons that appear essential for sustaining fat loss. The surprising discovery in mice could reveal new targets for developing even more effective obesity drugs.

science.title: A snake-headed vessel hints at a mysterious Roman cult
science.summary: The ancient Romans were a deeply religious and superstitious people, worshiping dozens of cults—some official and others secretive. One of these was dedicated to Sabazios, a deity from Thrace and Phrygia (regions spanning parts of the modern-day Balkans and Turkey).

science.title: Caught right-handed: Mystery of coiling snake embryos explained
science.summary: An international team led by Canadian researchers has found evidence explaining why snake embryos form a curious spiral. This ability to coil as embryos enables snakes to hatch with the longest bodies of all vertebrates.

science.title: How the Tasmanian tiger outfoxed its prey
science.summary: The Tasmanian tiger hunted more like a fox than its fearsome namesake, according to a new UniSC biomechanics study of predatory animals across the globe. The University of the Sunshine Coast-led research, published in BMC Ecology and Evolution, featured the thylacine in a comparison of 48 living and extinct predatory mammal species, from domestic dogs to African wildcats.

science.title: Rocky Mountain find reveals new funnel-web spider far from its Northwest relatives
science.summary: Researchers at the University of Idaho have identified a new species of spider in the mountains of northern Idaho and given it a name that pays tribute to the university itself: Hexura vandal. The spider belongs to a small group of funnel-web spiders related to tarantulas. Until now, only two species in this genus were known, both living hundreds of miles away in the coastal forests and mountains of Oregon and Washington.

science.title: JWST reveals likely Type II supernova from when universe was only 2 billion years old
science.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have identified one of the most distant exploding stars ever confirmed. The supernova, SN 2023aeaf, was found at a redshift of 3.195—so far away that its light has been traveling for roughly 11.7 billion years. The study, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Aug. 13, offers a close-up look at how massive stars die in the young universe's primitive, metal-poor conditions.

science.title: Chemists develop method for the synthesis of natural compounds with potential in medicine
science.summary: A team of scientists from the Department of Organic Chemistry at the Faculty of Science, Charles University, Prague, has reported a new method that simplifies the preparation of complex molecules. The work was published in the journal Organic Letters. Such molecules are related to natural compounds known for their anticancer and anti-inflammatory effects. The new approach could help scientists prepare different variants of these compounds and study their biological effects.

science.title: Human-driven fires have shaped the Amazonian forest for over 10,000 years
science.summary: New research is dismantling the longstanding myth of the "pristine" Amazon. A reconstruction of 10,000 years of Amazonian pyrogeography, based on 1,361 radiocarbon (¹⁴C) dates across 303 sites—including soil charcoal and burned archaeological material—shows that fire in the rainforest is almost exclusively a human-driven phenomenon, not a natural one.

science.title: Metamaterials may enable invisibility cloaks, thinner lenses and smarter wireless networks
science.summary: Who has not dreamed of an invisibility cloak like the one used by Harry Potter? It sounds like magic, but it could become reality with the help of so-called metamaterials. In the summer of 2026, some of the world's leading researchers in the field gathered in Umeå for a Nobel Symposium on metamaterials. The symposium was organized by Nicolò Maccaferri, associate professor at Umeå University. He studies these special materials, which over the past few decades have proven useful in fields ranging from telecommunications to medical technology.

science.title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launches
science.summary: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, transits the Sun during launch from the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Aug. 30, 2026. Roman is named after the agency’s first chief astronomer. Roman will survey billions of stars and galaxies with a field of view far larger than Hubble’s, […]

science.title: Why innovative 'bio‑materials' are still more sci‑fi than fashion revolution
science.summary: Walk around any major fashion exhibition and you might get the impression that biofabricated materials are about to transform fashion. Grown using living organisms, they're often showcased as the next generation of sustainable materials—promising alternatives to leather, polyester and other conventional textiles.

science.title: Flexible nanopores shed new light on Parkinson's and ALS
science.summary: In a promising milestone for nanotechnology, Constructor University has contributed to a study demonstrating self-assembling nanopores capable of detecting disease proteins associated with illnesses like Parkinson's and ALS.

science.title: Why the image of 'clean and green' is no longer enough for Australian agriculture exports
science.summary: Australia's agricultural exports have long traded on a simple label: clean and green.

science.title: Scientists discover two superconducting states hiding as one
science.summary: Scientists have uncovered hidden complexity inside two ultrathin superconductors that seemed much simpler than they really are. Niobium diselenide and tantalum disulfide appeared to have a single superconducting state, but highly sensitive measurements revealed that each actually contains two strongly interacting states working so closely together that they masquerade as one.

science.title: Physicists take Hall effect in a new direction
science.summary: Carnegie Mellon University scientists have uncovered a new phenomenon that challenges a longstanding assumption about how electronic materials respond to magnetic fields. The discovery broadens the fundamental understanding of the Hall effect, a principle widely used to measure the magnetic and electronic properties of materials.

science.title: AI streamlines search for new ceramics that generate electricity
science.summary: A tedious process of trial and error is normally required to discover ceramic materials that generate electricity under mechanical stress. Known as piezoelectric ceramics, these valuable next-generation materials can replace batteries that power small electronic devices, like sensors. To streamline the research process, a team led by materials science researchers at Penn State introduced a new framework that combines an existing artificial intelligence (AI) model with human expertise to uncover these materials. To test the new approach, researchers developed a new piezoelectric composite and incorporated it into an energy harvester, which converts vibrations or movements into electricity.

science.title: Americans are more likely to support religious exemption requests that align with their political beliefs
science.summary: The United States Constitution protects the free exercise of religion, meaning that religious exemptions can sometimes be granted if a law infringes on someone's sincerely held religious beliefs. But how do people decide whether someone else's religious exemption requests are legitimate? New research suggests that political ideology can play a key role in the court of public opinion.

science.title: The mystery of a well-traveled kissing bug
science.summary: On an August morning last year, an American couple soon to embark on a European river cruise awoke in a luxury hotel in Lisbon.

science.title: Fossil feet may be misleading scientists about human evolution
science.summary: Wild monkeys in West Africa can climb vertical tree trunks using foot flexibility scientists did not realize they possessed. The discovery challenges a key assumption about what the last common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees looked like and how it moved.

science.title: The paper that predicted the office apocalypse
science.summary: When an early draft of "Work from Home and the Office Real Estate Apocalypse," co-authored by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, the Earle W. Kazis and Benjamin Schore Professor of Real Estate at Columbia Business School, began circulating in 2022, it quickly became one of the most talked-about papers in real estate and urban economics.

science.title: Roman Commissioning
science.summary: Where is Roman? Roman is making its three-month journey from Earth to Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2, or L2. Along the way, Roman is undergoing a process called commissioning, where systems are turned on, adjusted, calibrated, and prepared for science operations. Commissioning is the time for scientists and engineers to make sure that Roman is performing […]

science.title: Physicists finally put Feynman's path integral to the test
science.summary: For nearly 80 years, physicists have relied on a thought experiment created by Richard Feynman to predict how quantum particles behave. For the first time, researchers in China have tested this trick directly in the lab.

science.title: Black fungus thriving in the midst of Ireland's whiskey boom
science.summary: Irish whiskey is one of Ireland's great export success stories. Exports were worth more than €930 million in 2025, with the country's much-loved spirit sold all over the world.

science.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope launches to reveal the Universe’s darkest secrets
science.summary: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has launched on a million mile journey to L2, where it will scan huge portions of the cosmos for clues about dark matter, dark energy, and distant worlds. With survey speeds roughly 1,000 times faster than Hubble and a torrent of 1.4 terabytes of data per day, Roman could uncover cosmic surprises astronomers have never seen before.

science.title: Not tiger, not wolf: Australian thylacine skull reveals a far different hunting style
science.summary: A new study led by Flinders University has flipped the historical narrative about Australia's thylacine, finding the native apex predator known as the "Tasmanian tiger" was significantly different from the wolves and wild dogs it was likened to before being hunted to extinction.

science.title: Rocky planets may have formed just 100 million years after the Big Bang
science.summary: Rocky planets may have been able to start forming just 100 million years after the Big Bang, thanks to enormous early supernovae that scattered planet-building elements across space. Simulations found enough solid material and water around a young star to suggest that Earth-like worlds could have appeared far earlier than previously believed.

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

Aproximativ 51 de kilometri de cale ferată nou modernizată și electrificată vor fi puși în exploatare pe Lotul 2 al proiectului Caransebeș - Timișoara - Arad. Contractul are o valoare de 1,916 miliarde de lei, fără TVA.

mix_items.title: Toamna începe cu vreme schimbătoare. Cum arată prognoza până pe 13 septembrie, în fiecare regiune din țară
mix_items.summary: Meteorologii anunță o vreme schimbătoare în următoarele două săptămâni, între 31 august - 13 septembrie, cu temperaturi care vor oscila în mai multe regiuni ale țării. După o răcorire la începutul lunii septembrie, temperaturile vor crește din nou în jurul datei de 5-6 septembrie, apoi vor scădea treptat, iar ploile vor reveni în mai multe zone.

mix_items.summary: The ancient Romans were a deeply religious and superstitious people, worshiping dozens of cults—some official and others secretive. One of these was dedicated to Sabazios, a deity from Thrace and Phrygia (regions spanning parts of the modern-day Balkans and Turkey).

mix_items.title: Caught right-handed: Mystery of coiling snake embryos explained
mix_items.summary: An international team led by Canadian researchers has found evidence explaining why snake embryos form a curious spiral. This ability to coil as embryos enables snakes to hatch with the longest bodies of all vertebrates.

mix_items.title: How the Tasmanian tiger outfoxed its prey
mix_items.summary: The Tasmanian tiger hunted more like a fox than its fearsome namesake, according to a new UniSC biomechanics study of predatory animals across the globe. The University of the Sunshine Coast-led research, published in BMC Ecology and Evolution, featured the thylacine in a comparison of 48 living and extinct predatory mammal species, from domestic dogs to African wildcats.

mix_items.title: Rocky Mountain find reveals new funnel-web spider far from its Northwest relatives
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Idaho have identified a new species of spider in the mountains of northern Idaho and given it a name that pays tribute to the university itself: Hexura vandal. The spider belongs to a small group of funnel-web spiders related to tarantulas. Until now, only two species in this genus were known, both living hundreds of miles away in the coastal forests and mountains of Oregon and Washington.

mix_items.title: No significant evidence for protection against cardiovascular outcomes with metformin in heart failure
mix_items.summary: Metformin did not significantly affect the risk of cardiovascular outcomes in patients with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and diabetes or at risk of diabetes. These were the main findings of the Met-HeFT trial and a meta-analysis presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026.

mix_items.title: JWST reveals likely Type II supernova from when universe was only 2 billion years old
mix_items.summary: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope have identified one of the most distant exploding stars ever confirmed. The supernova, SN 2023aeaf, was found at a redshift of 3.195—so far away that its light has been traveling for roughly 11.7 billion years. The study, published in The Astrophysical Journal on Aug. 13, offers a close-up look at how massive stars die in the young universe's primitive, metal-poor conditions.

mix_items.title: Chemists develop method for the synthesis of natural compounds with potential in medicine
mix_items.summary: A team of scientists from the Department of Organic Chemistry at the Faculty of Science, Charles University, Prague, has reported a new method that simplifies the preparation of complex molecules. The work was published in the journal Organic Letters. Such molecules are related to natural compounds known for their anticancer and anti-inflammatory effects. The new approach could help scientists prepare different variants of these compounds and study their biological effects.

mix_items.title: Human-driven fires have shaped the Amazonian forest for over 10,000 years
mix_items.summary: New research is dismantling the longstanding myth of the "pristine" Amazon. A reconstruction of 10,000 years of Amazonian pyrogeography, based on 1,361 radiocarbon (¹⁴C) dates across 303 sites—including soil charcoal and burned archaeological material—shows that fire in the rainforest is almost exclusively a human-driven phenomenon, not a natural one.

mix_items.title: An RNA molecule contributes to therapy resistance of triple negative breast cancer
mix_items.summary: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive type of breast cancer. Chemotherapy before or after surgery remains the standard treatment regimen for stage I–III TNBC. Only a small portion of patients can benefit from targeted therapy with PARP inhibitors because of BRCA mutations. However, resistance to chemotherapy or targeted therapy remains a major hurdle.

mix_items.title: Metamaterials may enable invisibility cloaks, thinner lenses and smarter wireless networks
mix_items.summary: Who has not dreamed of an invisibility cloak like the one used by Harry Potter? It sounds like magic, but it could become reality with the help of so-called metamaterials. In the summer of 2026, some of the world's leading researchers in the field gathered in Umeå for a Nobel Symposium on metamaterials. The symposium was organized by Nicolò Maccaferri, associate professor at Umeå University. He studies these special materials, which over the past few decades have proven useful in fields ranging from telecommunications to medical technology.

mix_items.title: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launches
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket, transits the Sun during launch from the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Aug. 30, 2026. Roman is named after the agency’s first chief astronomer. Roman will survey billions of stars and galaxies with a field of view far larger than Hubble’s, […]

mix_items.title: Popular sweeteners may leave effects that last for generations
mix_items.summary: Two widely used zero-calorie sweeteners, sucralose and stevia, may have effects that linger far longer than the sweet taste itself. In mice, researchers found that both sweeteners altered the gut microbiome, reduced beneficial compounds produced by gut bacteria, and changed the activity of genes involved in metabolism and inflammation. Some of those changes were also detected in later generations that had never consumed the sweeteners themselves.

mix_items.title: Why innovative 'bio‑materials' are still more sci‑fi than fashion revolution
mix_items.summary: Walk around any major fashion exhibition and you might get the impression that biofabricated materials are about to transform fashion. Grown using living organisms, they're often showcased as the next generation of sustainable materials—promising alternatives to leather, polyester and other conventional textiles.

mix_items.title: Trial results favor prasugrel over ticagrelor after coronary stenting
mix_items.summary: Prasugrel reduced major cardiovascular events to the same extent as ticagrelor but with lower major bleeding after coronary stenting in patients with acute coronary syndromes, according to results from the SWITCH SWEDEHEART trial presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026 and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.

mix_items.title: Flexible nanopores shed new light on Parkinson's and ALS
mix_items.summary: In a promising milestone for nanotechnology, Constructor University has contributed to a study demonstrating self-assembling nanopores capable of detecting disease proteins associated with illnesses like Parkinson's and ALS.

mix_items.title: Why the image of 'clean and green' is no longer enough for Australian agriculture exports
mix_items.summary: Australia's agricultural exports have long traded on a simple label: clean and green.

mix_items.title: T cell therapy shows promise in treating aggressive brain cancer
mix_items.summary: A new phase 1 clinical trial has found that an emerging immunotherapy is promising for treating recurrent glioblastoma, a highly aggressive and fatal brain cancer. Chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cell therapy is a form of immunotherapy that modifies an individual's own T cells (a type of immune cell) so they are better able to recognize and destroy cancer cells. The new clinical trial, the results of which were published Aug. 6 in Nature Medicine, focuses on a form of CAR-T therapy that trains these immune cells to target a protein known as B7-H3, which is highly prevalent in most glioblastomas.

mix_items.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.title: Scientists discover two superconducting states hiding as one
mix_items.summary: Scientists have uncovered hidden complexity inside two ultrathin superconductors that seemed much simpler than they really are. Niobium diselenide and tantalum disulfide appeared to have a single superconducting state, but highly sensitive measurements revealed that each actually contains two strongly interacting states working so closely together that they masquerade as one.

mix_items.title: Physicists take Hall effect in a new direction
mix_items.summary: Carnegie Mellon University scientists have uncovered a new phenomenon that challenges a longstanding assumption about how electronic materials respond to magnetic fields. The discovery broadens the fundamental understanding of the Hall effect, a principle widely used to measure the magnetic and electronic properties of materials.

mix_items.title: Virtual monitoring matches clinic care for heart-device patients
mix_items.summary: A virtual e-health system (VIRTUES) was as safe and effective as standard care for monitoring the function of cardiac implantable electronic devices, with the benefits of cost savings and patient satisfaction. These were the main findings of the VIRTUES trials presented in a Hot Line session at ESC Congress 2026.

mix_items.title: Targeting protein synthesis control regions may reduce seizures in genetic epilepsy
mix_items.summary: Targeting the control of protein synthesis in the KCNQ2 gene may serve as a potential disease-modifying strategy for patients with a genetic form of neonatal-onset epilepsy and impaired brain development, according to a Northwestern Medicine study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: AI streamlines search for new ceramics that generate electricity
mix_items.summary: A tedious process of trial and error is normally required to discover ceramic materials that generate electricity under mechanical stress. Known as piezoelectric ceramics, these valuable next-generation materials can replace batteries that power small electronic devices, like sensors. To streamline the research process, a team led by materials science researchers at Penn State introduced a new framework that combines an existing artificial intelligence (AI) model with human expertise to uncover these materials. To test the new approach, researchers developed a new piezoelectric composite and incorporated it into an energy harvester, which converts vibrations or movements into electricity.

mix_items.title: Scientists in France pinpoint why STING pathway hasn't been harnessed for cancer therapy yet
mix_items.summary: Deep within the cellular landscape, a quiet failure was taking place, impeding a potentially successful form of cancer treatment. For years, scientists hoped an essential part of the innate immune system that detects foreign DNA in cellular cytoplasm—the STING pathway—could be harnessed for use in cancer immunotherapy.

mix_items.title: Americans are more likely to support religious exemption requests that align with their political beliefs
mix_items.summary: The United States Constitution protects the free exercise of religion, meaning that religious exemptions can sometimes be granted if a law infringes on someone's sincerely held religious beliefs. But how do people decide whether someone else's religious exemption requests are legitimate? New research suggests that political ideology can play a key role in the court of public opinion.

mix_items.title: Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth
mix_items.summary: A long-standing picture of brain evolution as newer, rational layers stacked on top of an ancient “lizard brain” may be deeply misleading. Researchers found that evolution instead appears to balance two competing styles of brain wiring, expanding one while shrinking the other depending on what an animal needs to survive.

mix_items.title: The mystery of a well-traveled kissing bug
mix_items.summary: On an August morning last year, an American couple soon to embark on a European river cruise awoke in a luxury hotel in Lisbon.

mix_items.title: Fossil feet may be misleading scientists about human evolution
mix_items.summary: Wild monkeys in West Africa can climb vertical tree trunks using foot flexibility scientists did not realize they possessed. The discovery challenges a key assumption about what the last common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees looked like and how it moved.

mix_items.title: The paper that predicted the office apocalypse
mix_items.summary: When an early draft of "Work from Home and the Office Real Estate Apocalypse," co-authored by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, the Earle W. Kazis and Benjamin Schore Professor of Real Estate at Columbia Business School, began circulating in 2022, it quickly became one of the most talked-about papers in real estate and urban economics.

mix_items.title: Roman Commissioning
mix_items.summary: Where is Roman? Roman is making its three-month journey from Earth to Sun-Earth Lagrange Point 2, or L2. Along the way, Roman is undergoing a process called commissioning, where systems are turned on, adjusted, calibrated, and prepared for science operations. Commissioning is the time for scientists and engineers to make sure that Roman is performing […]

mix_items.title: Physicists finally put Feynman's path integral to the test
mix_items.summary: For nearly 80 years, physicists have relied on a thought experiment created by Richard Feynman to predict how quantum particles behave. For the first time, researchers in China have tested this trick directly in the lab.

mix_items.title: Black fungus thriving in the midst of Ireland's whiskey boom
mix_items.summary: Irish whiskey is one of Ireland's great export success stories. Exports were worth more than €930 million in 2025, with the country's much-loved spirit sold all over the world.

mix_items.title: Professional gaming is brutal on the body—inside the growing field of treating esports injuries
mix_items.summary: Chinese esports player Jian "Uzi" Zi-hao was more than a star "League of Legends" player: He was so talented that his team structured its entire strategy around his abilities, funneling resources to him and another teammate, Shi "Ming" Sen-Ming, so the duo could lead the team to victory. Over the course of his career, he earned more than $500,000 in tournament prize money.

mix_items.title: Most women wear shoes that don't match their feet, study finds
mix_items.summary: Most women in a new RMIT University study wore shoe sizes that differed from the size indicated by their foot length, highlighting the limitations of conventional sizing systems in accounting for differences in foot width and shape. The study of 107 women found 72% wore a different size under U.S. sizing and 65% under EU sizing.

mix_items.title: New prediction tool could help increase uptake of heart failure medicines
mix_items.summary: A new heart failure (HF) treatment effect calculator could help overcome one of the largest barriers to effective heart failure care by predicting the expected effects of treatment on blood pressure, kidney function and potassium levels. The research, presented today at the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Congress and simultaneously published today in Nature Medicine, uses individual patient data from 38,753 participants across nine major heart failure trials.

mix_items.title: New guidelines aim to bring precision medicine to stroke rehabilitation
mix_items.summary: A University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM) stroke rehabilitation specialist helped develop new recommendations for studying molecular biomarkers associated with recovery from stroke. The new guidelines could help pave the way for precision rehabilitation approaches tailored to individual patients.

mix_items.title: Scientists find why the liver may not heal even after you stop drinking
mix_items.summary: Alcohol-related liver disease may trap damaged liver cells in a regenerative limbo, preventing the organ from rebuilding itself even after drinking stops. Researchers linked the problem to inflammation-driven RNA errors and identified a pathway that could potentially be targeted to restore liver repair.

mix_items.title: The unlikely rise of the sea shanty band
mix_items.summary: Sea shanties became an online craze, but these old working songs are doing more than filling dancefloors: they're connecting communities too The post The unlikely rise of the sea shanty band appeared first on Positive News .

mix_items.title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope launches to reveal the Universe’s darkest secrets
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has launched on a million mile journey to L2, where it will scan huge portions of the cosmos for clues about dark matter, dark energy, and distant worlds. With survey speeds roughly 1,000 times faster than Hubble and a torrent of 1.4 terabytes of data per day, Roman could uncover cosmic surprises astronomers have never seen before.

mix_items.title: Not tiger, not wolf: Australian thylacine skull reveals a far different hunting style
mix_items.summary: A new study led by Flinders University has flipped the historical narrative about Australia's thylacine, finding the native apex predator known as the "Tasmanian tiger" was significantly different from the wolves and wild dogs it was likened to before being hunted to extinction.

mix_items.title: Recording a rainforest before Indonesia’s new capital changes it
mix_items.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. In the forests around Pemaluan in East Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo, researchers led by Wendy Erb at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics in the U.S. have placed audio recorders on mountains, beside caves, and among […]

mix_items.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
mix_items.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

mix_items.title: Rocky planets may have formed just 100 million years after the Big Bang
mix_items.summary: Rocky planets may have been able to start forming just 100 million years after the Big Bang, thanks to enormous early supernovae that scattered planet-building elements across space. Simulations found enough solid material and water around a young star to suggest that Earth-like worlds could have appeared far earlier than previously believed.

mix_items.title: Scientists may have found a shortcut to calorie restriction’s anti-aging benefits
mix_items.summary: Moderate calorie restriction lowered an immune protein called C3 that appears to help drive chronic inflammation as the body ages. Blocking the same protein reduced age related inflammation in mice, raising the possibility that future treatments could mimic some benefits of calorie restriction without severe dieting.

mix_items.title: Turmeric compound may protect blood vessels from diabetes damage
mix_items.summary: A compound found in turmeric may help protect blood vessels from some of the damage caused by Type 1 diabetes. In rats, curcumin reduced inflammation, improved cellular signaling, and restored vascular health to levels resembling those of nondiabetic animals. The results hint at a possible new way to reduce the long-term cardiovascular risks of diabetes, but human trials are still needed.

mix_items.title: A missing color in indoor light may help prevent myopia
mix_items.summary: A wavelength of light largely missing from indoor LEDs may play an important role in protecting developing eyes from nearsightedness. Researchers found that indigo light completely prevented myopia in tree shrews, whose eyes share important similarities with human eyes. The discovery raises the possibility that future indoor lighting could be redesigned to more closely mimic sunlight and potentially reduce childhood myopia.

mix_items.title: Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells
mix_items.summary: Early-life stress may physically alter how DNA is packaged in the brain, leaving stress-related genes primed to activate more easily years later. In mice, researchers were able to block this effect, preventing the heightened anxiety and stress sensitivity that otherwise appeared in adulthood.

mix_items.title: This weight-loss hormone may protect the liver even without weight loss
mix_items.summary: A hormone already known for curbing appetite and supporting weight loss may have a surprising second job: protecting the liver from inflammation and scarring. Researchers at McMaster University found that GDF15 activates a previously unknown brain-to-liver pathway that triggers the release of glucocorticoids, helping calm immune activity in the liver.

mix_items.title: AI may know how you’ll respond to a vaccine before you get it
mix_items.summary: AI may be able to predict how strongly someone will respond to a vaccine before they receive it. By analyzing antibody patterns in more than 4,000 people, researchers found signs of “immune readiness” that helped distinguish strong responders from weak ones. Surprisingly, even some healthy people responded poorly, while some immunosuppressed people mounted strong responses.

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover how gut bacteria “train” the intestine to fight inflammation
mix_items.summary: A compound made when gut bacteria break down dietary fiber may do more than briefly calm inflammation—it could leave a lasting protective “memory” in the gut. Northwestern Medicine researchers found that butyrate can reprogram intestinal lining cells so they continue encouraging anti-inflammatory immune responses even after the compound is gone. In mice, this effect boosted production of the immune-calming molecule IL-10 and reduced the severity of colitis-like disease.

mix_items.title: Ozempic does something unexpected to the brain’s hunger neurons
mix_items.summary: Ozempic may work in the brain in almost the opposite way scientists expected, activating hunger-linked neurons that appear essential for sustaining fat loss. The surprising discovery in mice could reveal new targets for developing even more effective obesity drugs.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
